name: Metehan Yeşilyurt
text:
Black Friday is in 2 days. Most AI search work takes longer than that, but a few things are still worth doing this week. I just published a report you might want to check. 

I looked at how ChatGPT, Google AI Overviews and AI Mode answered US shopping questions from Oct 12 to Nov 19. Here is what you can still do in 2 days:

1. Put your deals on the pages AI already finds. ChatGPT only adds "Black Friday" to its searches when the shopper asks for it (98% vs under 1%). Someone asking for "the best cordless vacuum" on Friday gets a normal search. So add the deal to your best-of and review pages, not only to your Black Friday landing page.

2. Check your offers at the big retailers. In the US, Walmart has 13% of ChatGPT's product card merchant slots. Amazon has less than 0.1% on all three engines. If your products sell at Walmart, Target or Best Buy, make sure the price and the deal are right there today. Walmart is leading at the moment and they just released integrations with shopping agents. 

3. If you run coupon pages, ask for codes tied to your site. ChatGPT now shows coupon codes in a deal card with a Copy code button, and Google writes the codes into the answer. A shopper who copies the code never clicks your link, so a cookie-based affiliate deal may not pay you.

Bonus: Publishers. Know which publishers each LLM/engine trusts. On ChatGPT, Condé Nast leads (Vogue, Allure, Wired, GQ). On AI Overviews, Ziff Davis leads (CNET, PCMag, Mashable). If one of their reviews already features your product, ask them to add your Black Friday & Cyber Monday price. 

Analyzing the trends is super easy if you're using Peec AI already. 

Full study with all the insights in comment  👇
sum: Metehan Yeşilyurt checked US shopping answers in ChatGPT, AIOs and AI Mode. ChatGPT adds 'Black Friday' to its searches only when the shopper asks, and Walmart holds 13% of ChatGPT's product card merchant slots.

name: Liam Dunne
text:
I've seen a few people saying Reddit is overhyped for AEO because citations have fallen off a cliff. Our research team analyzed 291,607 ChatGPT citations and investigated how it retrieves Reddit content, and there’s a big piece missing from that narrative.

Let me start off by saying a decline has effectively happened. Reddit's share of ChatGPT citations dropped from 0.35% to 0.12% between our 2025 and 2026 measurements 

But citations are only the “visible” part of it. So we looked at the retrieval data, and found this:

→ ChatGPT has a dedicated retrieval mechanism for Reddit

This means that rather than competing with other websites in regular search results, Reddit has its own route that can pull up to 12 threads into ChatGPT's reading list 

→ ChatGPT has become much more selective about when it uses Reddit

In our latest tests, ChatGPT retrieved Reddit in roughly 1/4 search turns (vs almost in every query last year). It also comes up primarily when people ask for opinions, experiences and recommendations. I.e., "What do people think about ZoomInfo's data accuracy?"

→ When ChatGPT reads Reddit, it frequently cites it

Reddit was cited on 73% of search turns where ChatGPT read its content. At the individual page level, Reddit's citation rate was 29%, which is roughly in line with the 31% average across other sources

TL;DR, the decline in overall citations has more to do with ChatGPT retrieving Reddit for fewer types of questions, and not because it’s less relevant across the board so I'd tread lightly about completely dismissing Reddit.

What I would DO if I were a marketer at a B2B SaaS company:

(1) Avoid making decisions based on citation volume alone. Look at what ChatGPT retrieves for the questions your buyers are asking 

(2) Identify the buyer questions that trigger Reddit retrieval. Test prompts where buyers ask about real-world experiences, product reliability, implementation challenges, alternatives and customer satisfaction

(3) Build a Reddit strategy around the threads where your target customers discuss the problems your product solves with real, valuable comments

Find the full research in the comments or DM me if you have any qs.
sum: Discovered Labs analyzed 291,607 ChatGPT citations. Reddit's share fell from 0.35% to 0.12%, but ChatGPT has its own route that pulls up to 12 Reddit threads, now in about 1 in 4 search turns.

name: Anastasiia Andriienko
text:
Cloudflare was blocking Googlebot.And the impact went far beyond a few HTTP 403 errors 🤖

In October, I investigated a technical SEO issue where a website's security configuration was preventing Googlebot from accessing important pages.
After a bot attack, the developer tightened Cloudflare's bot protection.
But legitimate search engine crawlers were getting blocked too.

Here's what Google Search Console showed on October 28, before the fix:

• The homepage and key category pages were reported as "URL is not on Google". Live URL Inspection returned HTTP 403.
• Google couldn't fetch robots.txt.
• The XML sitemap index couldn't be fetched.
• As of October 24, Crawl Stats showed around 409,000 "other client error (4XX)" responses, with daily errors reaching approximately 60,000.
• On October 25 (a Sunday), the website recorded just 476 clicks and 8,175 impressions.

Googlebot couldn't reliably access the website, disrupting crawling and indexing.

The investigation led to Cloudflare's security rules.
An exception for known bots was already in place, but it wasn't enough to prevent other security restrictions from blocking Googlebot.
Together with the developer, we adjusted the configuration on October 28 to restore access for verified search engine crawlers.
We then checked HTTP responses for verified Google requests and monitored crawling in Search Console.

After the fix:
4XX crawl errors dropped to nearly zero within two days.
Googlebot resumed crawling affected pages, and organic search performance gradually began to improve.

📈 As of November 25, the latest seven-day data shows:
• 4.85K clicks (+9% week over week)
• 130K impressions (+4%)

Clicks are recovering, while impressions remain below pre-incident levels.

These numbers don't prove that the Cloudflare fix alone caused the improvement. But restoring crawler access was a necessary step.

The website continued working normally for regular visitors. It returned HTTP 200 to users while returning HTTP 403 to Googlebot.

You can spend weeks improving content and fixing internal links. But if Googlebot can't access those pages, it can't properly crawl the changes.

‼️For anyone using Cloudflare, I'd recommend checking how security rules affect verified search engine crawlers, especially after changing bot protection settings.

And don't rely only on whether the website loads in your browser. Check the HTTP responses Googlebot actually receives and monitor GSC Crawl Stats.

Have you ever seen Cloudflare block Googlebot despite having an exception for known bots?

#TechnicalSEO #Cloudflare #Googlebot #EcommerceSEO
sum: Tighter Cloudflare bot rules blocked Googlebot on a client site. GSC showed 403 errors, no robots.txt or sitemap fetch, and about 409,000 4XX crawl responses.

name: Mahendra C.
text:
𝗔𝗜 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘁𝗿𝗶𝗯𝘂𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝗷𝘂𝘀𝘁 ~𝟭% 𝗼𝗳 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰 𝗮𝗰𝗿𝗼𝘀𝘀 𝟰𝟵 𝘄𝗲𝗯𝘀𝗶𝘁𝗲𝘀. 𝗕𝘂𝘁 𝗶𝘁 𝗴𝗲𝗻𝗲𝗿𝗮𝘁𝗲𝗱 ~𝟮.𝟱% 𝗼𝗳 𝗲𝗖𝗼𝗺𝗺𝗲𝗿𝗰𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗻𝘂𝗲.

That's one of the more interesting findings from our recent research at Botpresso published by Nitin Manchanda

We wanted to understand what actually changes when moving from traditional SEO to AEO (Answer Engine Optimisation). So we looked beyond theories and tested real-world data across websites, AI platforms and experiments.

Some findings were particularly interesting.

📊 𝗪𝗵𝗮𝘁 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝗿𝗲𝘃𝗲𝗮𝗹𝗲𝗱:
→ 𝗔𝗜 𝘀𝗲𝗮𝗿𝗰𝗵 𝘁𝗿𝗮𝗳𝗳𝗶𝗰: ~1% of total sessions but ~2.5% of eCommerce revenue across 49 websites over 30 days.
→ 𝗡𝗶𝗰𝗵𝗲 𝗯𝗿𝗮𝗻𝗱𝘀: AI search contributed up to 16% of revenue for some smaller, specialised brands.
→ 𝗕𝟮𝗕 𝗰𝗼𝗻𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀: AI search visitors converted at 16.48%, compared to 7.27% from organic search. That's approximately 2.3x higher.
→ 𝗖𝗵𝗮𝘁𝗚𝗣𝗧 𝗰𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀: 86% of the citations we analysed came from official platform documentation.
→ 𝗚𝗲𝗺𝗶𝗻𝗶 𝗰𝗶𝘁𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀: 57% of citations pointed to just four pages.
→ 𝗚𝗼𝗼𝗴𝗹𝗲 𝗔𝗜 𝗢𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘃𝗶𝗲𝘄𝘀: 32% of citations came from platforms such as YouTube, LinkedIn, Medium, Quora, Instagram and Reddit.

🧪 𝗪𝗲 𝗮𝗹𝘀𝗼 𝘁𝗲𝘀𝘁𝗲𝗱 𝘀𝗼𝗺𝗲 𝗽𝗼𝗽𝘂𝗹𝗮𝗿 𝗔𝗘𝗢 𝗮𝘀𝘀𝘂𝗺𝗽𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻𝘀. 𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗿𝗲𝘀𝘂𝗹𝘁𝘀 𝘄𝗲𝗿𝗲 𝘂𝗻𝗲𝘅𝗽𝗲𝗰𝘁𝗲𝗱.
→ llms.txt: We observed 823 LLM bot requests in our server logs, but zero requests to /llms.txt.
→ 𝗦𝗰𝗵𝗲𝗺𝗮-𝗼𝗻𝗹𝘆 𝗳𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘀: Across four test pages, neither ChatGPT nor Claude returned the facts we had made available exclusively through structured data.

So, should businesses abandon traditional SEO and start optimising exclusively for AI search?
𝗔𝗯𝘀𝗼𝗹𝘂𝘁𝗲𝗹𝘆 𝗻𝗼𝘁.

Our research reinforces an important distinction.

𝗦𝗘𝗢 𝗮𝗻𝗱 𝗔𝗘𝗢 𝘀𝗵𝗮𝗿𝗲 𝘁𝗵𝗲 𝘀𝗮𝗺𝗲 𝘁𝗲𝗰𝗵𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹 𝗳𝗼𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗮𝘁𝗶𝗼𝗻:
• Crawlability and indexability
• Site architecture and internal linking
• Content quality and relevance
• Clear, accessible information
The difference lies in what happens beyond that foundation.

Traditional SEO focuses heavily on rankings, clicks and organic visibility.

AEO adds another dimension: whether your content gets retrieved, understood, cited and mentioned in AI-generated answers.
And that means your website is no longer the only surface that matters. Your brand's presence across documentation, communities, publications, social platforms and other authoritative sources also deserves attention.

𝗧𝗵𝗲 𝗳𝘂𝘁𝘂𝗿𝗲 𝗶𝘀𝗻'𝘁 𝗦𝗘𝗢 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘂𝘀 𝗔𝗘𝗢. 𝗜𝘁'𝘀 𝘂𝗻𝗱𝗲𝗿𝘀𝘁𝗮𝗻𝗱𝗶𝗻𝗴 𝗵𝗼𝘄 𝗯𝗼𝘁𝗵 𝘄𝗼𝗿𝗸 𝘁𝗼𝗴𝗲𝘁𝗵𝗲𝗿.

Read the full research, methodology, experiments and findings:
https://lnkd.in/dzZ6suh2

#SEO #AEO #GEO #AISearch #Botpresso

name: Olivia Moore
text:
Agents may be the biggest distribution opportunity ever - working 24/7 on our behalf, with our wallets. How do you attract their attention? We Andreessen Horowitz partnered with The Prompting Company on more than 10,000 runs across the four leading agents - our takeaways 👇

1. Lean in to use cases where your product "spikes". Agents have default picks (hero products) for general requests, and it's hard to break into this set. But, they're highly susceptible to marketing around specific use cases and personas - which may seem niche, but can add up. When asked for graphic design software, agents picked Canva in 78% of cases...this flipped to 100% for Adobe when the user specified pro-level output.

2. Optimize for agent crawlers, not (just) human eyeballs. Agents look at a limited # of product pages before making a decision. They need to immediately be able to grok what you do, the cost, and what makes you unique. For software, this likely means having an API / MCP and docs. For physical products or services, this means no complex UI (even if it looks cool!) that takes the agents more time and tokens to navigate. 

3. Agents ruthlessly optimize value. Unlike humans, they'll fully load the cost of your product - subscription terms, return/cancel policy, warranties, shipping, etc. Things that work on people (ex. low first year price, spike after) will be sniffed out and penalized by agents. And, if you sell your product in more than one place, be cognizant of the fact that the agent will find the most efficient place to buy it. 

4. Each agent has its own tastes. Muse is price-conscious, while Dots looks for the best reviewed option...even at a premium. If you're a smaller business, Instinct may be your best bet, while GrokBot is a heavy Amazon customer. In the medium/long term, connectors and plug-ins may win. And, protocols are emerging around tokenized identity, fraud, and payments that will be important to adapt to. Platforms like Shopify are already doing a lot of this heavy lifting for their customers

name: Josh Blyskal
text:
Do citation chips in ChatGPT actually drive traffic? Since May 7, when ChatGPT started hyperlinking brand names inline, I think everyone (me included) assumed the chips rly didn’t. I pulled 4,954 human visits from ChatGPT to our own site last week to see where people actually land, here’s what’s up:

- 38% of visits landed on pages that mostly show up as citation chips: and they land on 100s of different pages (guides, research, product pages, best-of lists)

- No single one of those pages got more than ~2%, so it’s a very very long tail

- 50% of visits landed on pages ChatGPT cites inline (47% on the homepage, 3% on other pages)

- The rest of people: 6% landed on the pricing page, which shows up both ways, and 6% on other pages

__________

So what's up here?

ChatGPT pulls the value out of your guides and comparison pages and puts it right in the answer, so those pages are already doing their job by informing the answer and getting cited.

I honestly assumed that’s where their job ended, bc nobody clicks the footnotes, right?

Well, 38% of visits says people still go check the details for themselves.

My mental framework is that the two citation styles go hand in hand: the content in the chips informs the answer, so it has a say in whether you get mentioned inline at all.

And the traffic from those chips is an added bonus (esp if you also assumed they weren’t rly driving any).

__________

So you can drive traffic in two ways:

1.) by being visible in the answer, through the inline link
2.) by getting cited, through the chips

As marketers, I think the next steps are pretty simple:

1.) Pull your ChatGPT sessions by landing page and look at the split between homepage and other pages (roughly: how much comes from being named in the answer vs being cited by it)
2.) Open a few of your long-tail pages as if you just clicked through from an answer: do they say who you are, and is there anywhere to go next?

FWIW this is one site (ours), and ChatGPT traffic is still a small slice of anyone’s total, so this is very much a sense check and something to use as a touchpoint.

What share of your ChatGPT traffic is from your homepage vs. elsewhere? 👀
sum: Profound checked 4,954 visits from ChatGPT to its own site. 38% landed on pages that show up as citation chips, so the chips do send traffic.

My favorite (actionable) data source for a GEO content plan is the citations list for the prompts we track.

 ✅ Cited domains show which websites & platforms dominate for each AI engine (I usually focus on AI Overviews and ChatGPT).
 ✅ Cited URLs show you the exact topics and content formats that get picked up.

👉 From there, you can see how much coverage each topic and content format has, so you know what to prioritize:

 1️⃣ What new pieces to create or what to update/optimize on your own website
 2️⃣  Which offsite actions to take (the most important part for AI search)

For our own website(s), I still build every content plan on a healthy SEO foundation: business relevance, search demand data, and SERP-based clustering.

❗ If you only follow AI source data with your own website, you can put your Google performance at risk because of cannibalization.

This trap is common on product websites, where two types of pages can cover the same top feature query: a feature landing page and a listicle of top tools (e.g., an "AI video generator" landing page vs. a "best AI video generators" listicle). 

 👉 AI search usually benefits from having both pages, since LLMs get more sources to pull from. In Google, though, the two pages will likely compete for the same queries, so SERP & your historical performance data should decide which one you build.

🟢 And the most fundamental source for any organic content plan: your customer data. AI search is still a black box when it comes to what users actually ask, so lean heavily on call recordings, input from your customer-facing teams and discussions on UGC platforms like Reddit. It works for SEO and GEO, and it also works for your users and your business.
sum: Anastasia Kotsiubynska builds GEO content plans from the cited domains and cited URLs of tracked prompts. She warns that AI source data alone can cause cannibalization and hurt Google performance.

name: Josh Blyskal
text:
I'm open-sourcing a bit of Profound's data. You ever see all these headlines and charts about global citation share shifts “this property is up 1%, that one’s down 2%” and everyone freaks out or takes a LinkedIn victory lap?

Every time, I just think: that’s like someone announcing the planetary average temperature today is 38°F (3°C for the Celsius folks) and saying, “Go figure out how to dress this morning.” Maybe it makes for good headlines. But it doesn’t actually tell you if you’ll freeze walking to the train or if you’ll be sweating by lunch.

Because at the end of the day, you need the weather for your 𝘀𝗽𝗲𝗰𝗶𝗳𝗶𝗰 𝗰𝗶𝘁𝘆, not some planetary average. And for AEO, the only thing that matters is 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗮𝗰𝘁𝘂𝗮𝗹 𝘃𝗲𝗿𝘁𝗶𝗰𝗮𝗹, 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝗿𝗲𝗮𝗹 𝗻𝗶𝗰𝗵𝗲, what’s happening for 𝘆𝗼𝘂𝗿 𝘀𝗹𝗶𝗰𝗲 of the industry. You can have 80° on average globally; your market might still be under snow.

Look, I could’ve posted a 2% citation change headline this week, and sometimes you genuinely do want to know if something big shifted because major model updates really can change your channel strategy. But before you bring that number to your CMO, or get worked up about it yourself, ask: Did anything really move in your vertical? Did the local forecast change for your business, or is the story just about the planetary average?

As marketers, it’s just good to remember that before we alarm, before we report up, we should always check our actual niche, or our real category. It might look like spring globally, but you might still be snowed in.

So, I’m releasing my own verticalized data today: it has the biggest citation share changers by answer engine, per vertical, for the last month or so (a sample of our DS, so no, this is not representative of “Profound’s whole dataset”) but I want to share it with you as a simple repo. The link is in the comments. Take the file, remix it, dig in, and actually see what matters in your vertical and region.

Because your local forecast should always beat the global average when you need to decide what to do next 👀 | 12 comments on LinkedIn
sum: Profound's Josh Blyskal says a global citation share change of 1% or 2% tells you little. Check what moved in your own vertical before you report a shift to a client.

name: Darren Shaw
text:
What happens when you block Google’s AI features from using your website content?
Cyrus Shepard tested what happens when you opt your website out of  Google's AI Overviews and AI Mode features, and here’s what he found:

1. AI impressions immediately dropped to zero
2. AI impressions were estimated to have a 0.9% click-through rate

Ok, so this is expected, but Cyrus also found that regular organic clicks dropped too when AI features were disabled (what?!)

He calls this the "SERP Halo Effect”.

The idea is that the more places your brand appears on the search results page, the more likely someone is to click through to your website.

When people see your business mentioned in multiple places on the search results page, it builds trust. 

And that could make them more likely to click on your website, even if it's through a regular organic result rather than an AI citation.

So anyway, you probably don’t want to opt out of Google’s AI features.
sum: Cyrus Shepard opted a site out of AIOs and AI Mode. AI impressions dropped to zero, and regular organic clicks dropped too. Darren Shaw's advice: do not opt out of Google's AI features.

name: Jimmy Park
text:
FASCINATING. People are starting to treat Google Search like ChatGPT. 

Interesting data:

DataForSEO tracked the queries reaching 2,000+ websites from September 2025 to August 2026.

- 15+ word queries: 0.37% to 0.82% of queries on desktop, 0.04% to 0.17% on mobile.
- 5+ word queries: 29.3% to 34.8% of desktop queries.
- 3-word queries lost the most share, down 3.18 percentage points on desktop.

Short queries still dominate. 3- and 4-word queries are still about 47% of desktop queries combined.

But we are seeing a gradual shift in longer queries.

People used to type the fewest words possible and let Google guess from two to three keywords. Now, they're picking up new habits from LLM usage and explaining their situation into Google so they get a specific answer.

You can run this research yourself in Claude & Google Search Console:
1. Open Search Console → Performance → Search results. Click Date → Compare → Compare last 3 months year over year.

2. Add a filter. Query → Custom (regex) → Matches regex. Paste one pattern, export the CSV, then swap in the next pattern. Each export caps at 1,000 rows, so splitting by length gets you far more of your queries than one export.
→ ^\S+(\s+\S+)?$ for 1-2 words
→ ^(\S+\s+){2}\S+$ for 3 words
→ ^(\S+\s+){3}\S+$ for 4 words
→ ^(\S+\s+){4,8}\S+$ for 5-9 words
→ ^(\S+\s+){9,}\S+$ for 10+ words

3. Name each file by its length (3-words.csv). If a file hits 1,000 rows, export that length again split by device and name each file by length and device (3-words-mobile.csv).

4. Upload all the CSVs to Claude and paste this prompt:

"These are Google Search Console exports, one per query length. The file name gives the length, and the device if I split it. Each file compares the last 3 months with the same 3 months last year. Remove any query that contains my brand name ([your brand]) from every file. Use code for all the counting.

Then:
→ Add the device files together for the same length.
→ For each length group, show the number of queries and total impressions in both periods.
→ Show each length group's share of total impressions in both periods, and the change in percentage points.
→ Give me the average words per query, weighted by impressions, for each period.
→ Flag any file with exactly 1,000 rows as cut off and tell me how that affects the result.
→ Answer in one line. Is my query length going up, down, or flat?
→ Use only the numbers in the files."

Happy to discuss results!
sum: DataForSEO data from 2,000+ sites shows longer Google queries. Queries of 5+ words grew from 29.3% to 34.8% of desktop queries in a year, as people search Google the way they prompt ChatGPT.

name: Dan Hinckley
text:
SEO & GEO Case Study: Google's AI now recommends this local business in 94% of its answers. Before, rarely if ever.

It started with SEO.

I don't believe a local business can get good AI results without a solid SEO plan. You have to be found first by search engines. Then your pages have to give the AI models enough details so it can generate solid answers for everything a user may be looking for.

We tested that on a local services business in 11 U.S. cities, in two steps.

Step one: get found.
Titles, descriptions, headings and 125 image descriptions. all the standard SEO best practices so Google can find and read every page.

Step two: give AI what it's looking for.
 - Match the intent. One search is really several questions: price, what's included, who it's for, where, who teaches. Google AI Overviews & ChatGPT extract just the sections of your page that it believes is likely to have what the user needs, so providing all the detail in the right places makes a difference. 
 - Analyze the query fan-out. AI asks the questions behind the query. We answered 55 of them for the business's most important revenue driving queries & prompts.
- Be specific. Real prices. Named neighborhoods and venues. Credentials about the business and the founders. Details an AI can easily consume and verify.

The results, two months after relaunch:
• 35 popular searches in Google's top 3. In August, none.
• 5× the monthly clicks from those top spots.
• Recommended in 94% of Google's AI answers. Cited in 95%.

More traffic from search. AI recommending the business by name. That is the path to more leads and revenue, which is what every local business is looking for.

GEO doesn't replace SEO. It takes great SEO past the keyword or topic, into the user's full need and the verification an AI does before it recommends you.

The charts are in the slides. The full study, written with Clara Sherman, can be found on our website.
sum: A local services business went from rare mentions to 94% of Google's AI answers, tested in 11 US cities. Dan Hinckley says it started with SEO: get found first, then give each page enough detail for AI models to answer from.

name: Ruben Remy
sub: Freelance SEO and AI Innovation Consultant
text:
Did you know Google BigQuery has an MCP server?

I’ve started setting it up for clients so they can ask questions about their own data in Claude or ChatGPT. Google Search Console, Google Analytics, and internal data that's kept in BigQuery. 

The Bigquery MCP makes it super easy for professionals to get questions answered about their data and offers their personal Oauth login with their Google account. It offers fine-grained access controls so users can only access what they are allowed. Most stakeholders should be read-only.

 💡 A few things I learned while setting it up:

1. Give them BigQuery Job User and MCP Tool User on the project, and Data Viewer only on the datasets they may read. A project-wide Data Viewer grant opens every table, so that's likely not what you want.

2. The tools require a project ID. Put it in the connector name or the first instruction. The assistant will otherwise not pick it up and would ask the oblivious user for it.

3. Write table and column descriptions/definitions in BigQuery. That is the definition the assistant reads while looking at the data. This is the simplest version of your "semantic layer". There are other options, but start here and it might be enough.

4. Create a separate OAuth client for the assistant, and mark it as a client for an AI agent. Don’t reuse the client that signs people into a dashboard. GCP offers a checkbox for that which you will see when setting up the Oauth client.

5. The user's email account with which they have a e.g. Claude account, is the same email that needs to get MCP access in Google Cloud. If the email addresses are not matching, then the claude agent cannot authenticate.

Do you need help with AI innovation at your company?
Besides SEO, this year I've been offering AI innovation and agentic acceleration as a service as well. Q1 2027 I will be able to help another Dutch company out, so feel free to ask! | 18 comments on LinkedIn

name: Lars Lofgren
sum: Base your 2027 SEO and GEO budget on which of 3 performance buckets your site is in.
text:
If you're deciding how to allocate your SEO/GEO budget for 2027, I'd base it on which of the 3 buckets that your site currently falls into (based on your 2026 performance).

I've had the fortune of working on a bunch of epic domains in the past few years. Huge brands, monster DRs, endless traffic, major budgets. Even in this cohort, SEO performance varies a lot. I have my suspicions for what causes this difference but that's another post for another time.

Roughly, every program has ended up in 1 of 3 buckets.

1) Google loves you = changes occur in weeks. New blog posts, updates, landing pages, technical fixes, whatever. In a lot of cases, you can see the impact in days. And it's not hard to show program progress over weeks. If this is you, go double down on whatever it is you're doing. I would, however, be careful about overspending on SEO. Somewhere in the $30-50K/month range is where I settle these days. After that, I spend on other channels. Increasing your budget from $10 to $20K? Definitely. Going from $50K to $100K? I probably wouldn't, even if things are going well. Overweighting on SEO can destroy the program.

2) Google likes you, doesn't love you though. Most changes take months to show real progress. You can definitely see progress YoY but nothing is a given. If this is you, I'd get your SEO budget into the $10-20K/month range at least. Take it seriously, keep building.

3) Google hates you. Feels like nothing ever works. If you squint, you can maybe see YoY progress but it all feels like a slog. Very common for sites that overweighted on SEO in the past (this is possible even for major brands). SEO got you into this mess, SEO will not get you out. For anyone in this bucket, I'd slash SEO budget to the bone. Maybe keep $5K/month for cleanup and basic updates. Cut everything else. Instead, dump all your budget into building other channels out (YouTube, Reddit, personal social profiles, etc). Ironically, this will make SEO a lot easier in the future.

name: Jimmy Park
sum: Stop chasing high-volume prompts. In 1,455 repeat prompts, the same brands came back only 7.49% of the time.
text:
AI search is NOT the same as SEO. I don't care about keywords or search volume. Instead, I look at AEO Determinants.

Before:
- Upload highest-volume visibility prompts into a tracker
- Read whichever citations come back
- Write articles chasing them
- Hope you’re now cited

This is NOT the right way to do AEO.

Instead of trying to show up for prompts, you need to intercept Determinants. 

Explained:

1. Don't chase high-volume visibility prompts
- Prompts are long-tail. Two buyers rarely type the same thing.
- There's no reliable way to measure prompt volume.
- Tracked prompts don't recommend the same brands consistently. We ran 1,455 prompts back to back across 14 industries, and the same set of brands came back only 7.49% of the time.

2. Instead, chase determinants that appear consistently
- A Determinant is a factor the model weighs before it makes a recommendation.
- We measured more than 659,000 AI responses to buying prompts. In 94.4% of ChatGPT's answers, 2 or more of 5 Determinants show up together:

a) Audience (59.8% of answers) - who's asking, by role, company size, and situation.
b) Use case (92.5%) - the job, plus what they already run and where they're based.
c) Selection criteria (83.9%) - price, features, quality, support, compliance.
d) Credibility (55.6%) - reviews, studies, certifications, expert mentions.
e) Brand association (at least 17.1%) - how tightly the model links you to the category.

- For example, I asked ChatGPT "My TV is getting old. Which one should I buy?" It then asked me about my budget & screen size (selection criteria), what I watch & how bright the room is (use case) before it recommended a solution.

3. How to take advantage of Determinants

a) Map the Determinants for your category
- Run buying prompts through ChatGPT and note every question it asks before it recommends.
- Sort each question into a Determinant. For example, a question about role or company size is audience.

b) Adjust your own pages for audience, use case, and selection criteria
- Imagine you run AEO for a payroll tool.
- For Audience, you would name every buyer type on your pages. Founders, HR managers, and accountants, from 3 employees to 3,000.
- For Use Case, you would write a section for each situation a buyer is in, then answer it. Think hiring in a second state or paying contractors.
- For Selection Criteria, you would publish what buyers compare you on. Think price per employee, whether tax filing is included, and how support works.

Google accidentally revealed how its AI search systems choose which sites to recommend and send traffic to.

Now that none of it is much of a secret anymore, let’s talk about it.
With the new Google Search rolling out as we speak, it has never been more important to understand how to maximize value from this marketing channel.

If you want to see where your site stands across Google, ChatGPT, Claude, Perplexity and broader AI search, you can do so for free here:

Let’s start from the beginning.

Metehan Yesilyurt, who previously went viral for his analysis of Perplexity’s ranking factors, recently broke down Google AI ranking factors in a fascinating blog post.

A lot of what he found also lines up with what SEO Stuff (seo-stuff.com) has been doing all year to get customers more traffic and sales.

Specifically with the done-for-you package:

https://lnkd.in/eZk7VPxz

Basically, Google sells much of the underlying retrieval infrastructure through Google Cloud Discovery Engine, also called Vertex AI Search.
By analyzing what Discovery Engine exposes, Yesilyurt was able to show how Google’s AI retrieval and ranking stack works.

The seven major signals he identified were Base Ranking, Gecko embedding similarity, Jetstream cross-attention relevance, BM25 keyword matching, predicted click-through rate, freshness and Boost/Bury rules.

In simpler terms, Google is combining traditional ranking signals with semantic similarity, deeper contextual relevance, keyword matching, engagement predictions, recency and manual business logic.

Discovery Engine exposes a maximum chunk size of 500 tokens, roughly 375 words, while ancestor headings can travel with each chunk and tables, images and page layouts can all be parsed with Gemini-enhanced understanding.

That means important ideas need to make sense inside relatively small, clearly labeled sections.

If your content is one massive wall of text, Google has a much harder job extracting the exact information it needs.

This is also why I keep talking about question-based headings, direct answers, clear comparisons and structured pages.

Additionally, Discovery Engine shows Google processing structured data using separate Searchable, Indexable and Retrievable settings.
Those can affect whether information can be found, used for filtering or ordering and surfaced by the model. Mind you, they are independent.

So a field can potentially influence retrieval or ranking without necessarily being displayed in exactly the same way.

That gives us a pretty significant clue about why structured data continues to matter as Google becomes more AI-driven.
